briefing.opening: Good morning/afternoon. We will now begin the climate briefing for September 30, 2026. Today, we will comprehensively examine the warning signs of the climate crisis emerging across the globe, the ongoing efforts towards carbon neutrality and renewable energy transition both domestically and internationally, and the various challenges surrounding climate action.

sections.title: 🔴 Climate Crisis Warning Signs Hitting the World and Changes in Domestic Ecosystems
sections.content: Today's news once again highlights the severe impact of climate change on various aspects of our lives on a global scale. Domestically, alongside news of 'Bukangyi' the shark, signaling rapid changes in the marine ecosystem [1], the shadow of climate change is extending to food prices, with 'autumn salted shrimp' disappearing ahead of the Kimjang season [2]. Furthermore, concerns are rising about adverse effects on local economies due to the onslaught of pine wilt disease [9], and the struggles of U.S. ski resorts facing reduced snow and visitor numbers [3] demonstrate how changes in natural environments, both domestic and international, can lead to economic setbacks. Internationally, climate change has also been identified as the biggest threat to the tourism industry [52], and reports that trees in a city in Southeast England are failing to adapt to the changing climate [54] reveal the overall vulnerability of ecosystems. Antarctic winter sea ice recorded its third lowest extent on record, raising alarms among scientists [84], and in the U.S., a surge in power outages amidst record heat is causing suffering for vulnerable populations [85], making the reality of the climate crisis palpable.

sections.title: 🌱 Domestic and International Efforts to Expand Renewable Energy and Accelerate Carbon Neutrality
sections.content: Amidst these crises, positive movements to address climate change are actively continuing both domestically and internationally. The Korean government plans to expand renewable energy generation capacity to 100GW by 2030 and innovate the power grid [6, 31, 32, 34, 35, 48], and specifically in the Honam region, power grid regulations that had been blocked for two years have been lifted, enabling the connection of 52GW of renewable energy [30, 37, 40, 41, 46]. Gyeongsangbuk-do Province is accelerating direct greenhouse gas reduction to achieve its 2050 carbon neutrality goal [14, 28], and local governments are undergoing active organizational restructuring, such as Taebaek City establishing a carbon neutrality department [22]. In various regions, including Geomdan-gu, Incheon, and Seogwipo City, resident-participatory carbon neutrality and resource circulation campaigns are actively underway [10, 12, 15, 16, 19, 23, 24, 25], and companies like Korea Zinc and NH Nonghyup Bank are also accelerating carbon neutrality at their production bases and resource circulation campaigns [17, 29]. Internationally, MIT's Climate Action Learning Lab is connecting research and policy for effective climate solutions [61], and collaborative efforts are expanding, such as CARICOM approving a new plan on health and climate change with PAHO [71].

sections.title: ⚠️ Challenges and Policy Hurdles Impeding Climate Action
sections.content: Despite positive efforts, many challenges and hurdles still exist for climate action. Domestically, while greenhouse gas reduction targets have been met, concerns have been raised that the pace of reduction has slowed for the third consecutive year [26], and worries have been voiced that the 'golden time' for renewable energy transition might be missed [38]. Notably, the fact that a significant portion of 'green bonds' issued by public power companies are also invested in fossil fuels like LNG [44, 50] raises questions about the sincerity of eco-friendly policies. The dominance of gas and nuclear power factions in domestic data center power policy discussions, coupled with low activity in the renewable energy sector [45], also highlights an imbalance in energy transition. Internationally, there was a case where New York State's Climate Change Superfund Act was dismissed by a federal court [60], and New Zealand is facing accusations of violating its climate change commitments with the EU [82], revealing difficulties in policy implementation. Furthermore, warnings that climate change could increase the spread of deadly viruses or rodent-borne diseases [58, 74], and research indicating it poses a major threat to skin health [78], suggest the widespread impact of the climate crisis on the public health sector.

sections.title: 📰 Expanding Climate Change Discourse in Culture, Law, and Research
sections.content: Climate change is now expanding beyond science and policy to become a broader societal discourse. U.S. Supreme Court Justice Alito's decision to recuse himself from major climate change lawsuits [51, 63, 64] demonstrates the significance of climate issues in the legal and political spheres. In the cultural sector, Tom Cruise's new film 'Digger' addresses climate change [55], and various reviews of the film either praise it as a 'Dr. Strangelove' for the climate change era [67, 73, 75, 81] or express disappointment with its message delivery [72, 76], indicating ongoing attempts to interpret climate change within popular culture. The release of a new multilingual album and the addition of a climate change specialist journalist [56, 62] also reflect this trend. Academically, Burlington County's Pinelands region is set to become a new focus for climate change research [57], and MIT's Climate Action Learning Lab has begun efforts to connect research and policy for effective solutions [61]. These developments clearly demonstrate that climate change is no longer an issue confined to a specific field, but a complex challenge that our entire society must collectively address and resolve.

briefing.closing: As we have reviewed in today's briefing, the climate crisis poses a tangible threat to our daily lives and global systems, but simultaneously, various efforts and new approaches are being explored to overcome it. This is a time that calls for continuous vigilance and bold action. This concludes today's climate briefing.
